items.title: Generating Synthetic Doctor-Patient Conversations for Long-form Audio Summarization
items.authors: Yanis Labrak(Idiap Research Institute); David Grünert(University of Zurich); Severin Baroudi(Idiap Research Institute; Université de Toulon, Aix Marseille Univ); Jiyun Chun(The Ohio State University); Pawel Cyrta(Stenograf); Sergio Burdisso(Idiap Research Institute); Ahmed Hassoon(Johns Hopkins University); David Liu(Colorado School of Mines); Adam Rothschild(Allegheny Health Network); Reed Van Deusen(University of Pittsburgh Medical Center); Petr Motlicek(Idiap Research Institute); Andrew Perrault(The Ohio State University); Ricard Marxer(Université de Toulon, Aix Marseille Univ; ILLS, CNRS); Thomas Schaaf(Solventum; Carnegie Mellon University)
items.abstract: Long-context audio reasoning is underserved in both training data and evaluation. Existing benchmarks target short-context tasks, and the open-ended generation tasks most relevant to long-context reasoning pose well-known challenges for automatic evaluation. We propose a synthetic data generation pipeline designed to serve both as a training resource and as a controlled evaluation environment, and instantiate it for first-visit doctor-patient conversations with SOAP note generation as the task. The pipeline has three stages—persona-driven dialogue generation, multi-speaker audio synthesis with overlap/pause modeling, room acoustics, and sound events, and LLM-based reference SOAP note production—built entirely on open-weight models. We release 8,800 synthetic conversations with 1.3k hours of corresponding audio and reference notes. Evaluating current open-weight systems, we find that cascaded approaches still substantially outperform end-to-end models.

items.title: Voice of India: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Real-World Speech Recognition in India
items.authors: Kaushal Bhogale(IIT Madras); Manas Dhir(Josh Talks); Amritansh Walecha(Josh Talks); Manmeet Kaur(Josh Talks); Vanshika Chhabra(Josh Talks); Aaditya Pareek(Josh Talks); Hanuman Sidh(Josh Talks); Sagar Jain(Josh Talks); Bhaskar Singh(Josh Talks); Utkarsh Singh(Josh Talks); Tahir Javed(IIT Madras); Shobhit Banga(Josh Talks); Mitesh M. Khapra(IIT Madras)
items.abstract: Existing Indic ASR benchmarks often use scripted, clean speech and leaderboard driven evaluation that encourages dataset specific overfitting. In addition, strict single reference WER penalizes natural spelling variation in Indian languages, including non standardized spellings of code-mixed English origin words. To address these limitations, we introduce Voice of India, a closed source benchmark built from unscripted telephonic conversations covering 15 major Indian languages across 139 regional clusters. The dataset contains 306230 utterances, totaling 536 hours of speech from 36691 speakers with transcripts accounting for spelling variations. We also analyze performance geographically at the district level, revealing disparities. Finally, we provide detailed analysis across factors such as audio quality, speaking rate, gender, and device type, highlighting where current ASR systems struggle and offering insights for improving real world Indic ASR systems.

items.title: CalliOpeNLP: A Standalone Digital Health Voice Data Collection Research Tool
items.authors: Brian Stasak(The University of Sydney); Rebecca Li(The University of Sydney); Antonia Chacon(The University of Sydney); Rebecca Black(The University of Sydney); Cate Madill(The University of Sydney)
items.abstract: Obstacles reported in manual health voice data collections include addressing compliance, annotation standards (e.g., labels, segmentation, transcription), security, interoperability (i.e., streamlined transfer), and in-person interaction bias. Automation is a logistical solution to mitigate these manual voice collection challenges. This paper introduces CalliOpeNLP, a new python-based open-source automated tool designed to support researchers working on clinical voice health data biobanks. While private commercial fee-based automated voice data collection software exist, CalliOpeNLP offers a free, standalone automated option which avoids unsecure data transfer. CalliOpeNLP includes computer-generated spoken- text instructions for 18 clinically validated voice tasks. CalliOpeNLP records, labels, and tracks patients' compliance using low latency voice-to-text transcript analytics. This tool provides a new practical application enhancing automated voice data collection capabilities.

items.title: Pronunciation and Intonation Structured Markup (PRISM): A Dataset for Australian English Pronunciation Feedback
items.authors: Olga Maxwell(University of Melbourne); Uy Thinh Quang(University of Melbourne); Debbie Loakes(University of Melbourne); Adele Gregory(University of Melbourne); Robert Turnbull(University of Melbourne)
items.abstract: While automated speech technologies for pronunciation learning are increasingly used, most tools offer limited feedback and lack scientific grounding. Phonetic variability in ESL speech and world Englishes is often ignored. We developed a curated dataset to support personalised feedback for Australian English pronunciation. Word-level forced alignment and manual annotation were applied to a demographically stratified subset of the CommonVoice corpus. Linguistically informed coding classes, such as vowels and tune types, were used to label “errors” (pronunciation differences from AusEng). This paper outlines the scientifically grounded annotation framework, presenting preliminary findings on error patterns across three accent groups: Hong Kong, South Asia, Indonesia. We also address challenges in using open data, including demographic imbalance. This work highlights collaboration between phonetics and computer science and provides an open-access dataset with a transparent framework.

items.title: Collection and Curation of a Spontaneous Multilingual Speech Corpus for Low-Resource Himalayan Languages
items.authors: Abhijit Sinha(National Institute of Technology); Subham Kutum(National Institute of Technology); Udara Laxman Kumar(National Institute of Technology); Paban Sapkota(National Institute of Technology); Hemant Kumar Kathania(National Institute of Technology)
items.abstract: Advancing speech technology for underrepresented languages requires carefully collected and well-documented data resources. In this work, we introduce a spontaneous multilingual speech corpus consisting of 320 native speakers of Bodo, Dzongkha, Gorkhali (Nepali), and Sherpa. These languages span the Tibeto-Burman and Indo-Aryan families and include both tonal and non-tonal systems. The corpus contains spontaneous speech recorded under consistent recording and curation protocols. We describe the participant selection process, recording design, and metadata organization used to maintain consistency across languages. Acoustic analysis highlights systematic differences in pitch, energy, and temporal dynamics among the languages. In addition, language identification experiments show that these distinctions remain learnable, achieving up to 92.95% accuracy and demonstrating the usefulness of the corpus for computational documentation and modeling of linguistically diverse speech communities.

items.title: Spontaneous Dialect-Aware Speech Corpus for Low-Resource Dakhini, A Southern Indo-Aryan Language: Methods, Challenges, and Insights
items.authors: Anindita Mondal(IIIT Hyderabad); Priyanka Kommagouni(Independent Researcher)
items.abstract: Dakhini, a contact variety spoken in the Deccan region of India, remains severely underrepresented in curated speech resources despite widespread conversational use. This work presents a data-centric study aimed at informing systematic Dakhini speech corpus development. Using telephonic conversational recordings, we examine factors relevant to corpus development, including context-driven code-switching and speaker variation across gender and educational backgrounds. Phonological reductions, auxiliary omission, and participial variation are observed in spontaneous speech, while formal contexts trigger shifts toward standardized Hindi/Urdu forms. These patterns highlight the importance of speaker stratification and dialect-aware annotation when curating low-resource conversational datasets. Our findings provide guidelines for developing Dakhini speech corpora and lay groundwork for dialect-sensitive ASR and conversational modeling in under documented language varieties.

items.title: Toward Multimodal Industrial Fault Analysis: A Single-Speed Chain Conveyor Dataset with Audio and Vibration Signals
items.authors: Zhang Chen(Duke Kunshan University); Yucong Zhang(Wuhan University; The Chinese University of Hong Kong (Shenzhen)); Xiaoxiao Miao(Duke Kunshan University); Ming Li(The Chinese University of Hong Kong (Shenzhen); Wuhan University)
items.abstract: We introduce a multimodal industrial fault analysis dataset collected from a single-speed chain conveyor (SSCC) system, targeting system-level fault detection in production lines. The dataset consists of multimodal signals, including three audio and four vibration channels. It covers normal operation and four representative fault types under multiple speeds, loads, and both clean and realistic factory-noise conditions reproduced on-site. It is explicitly designed to support channel-wise analysis and multimodal fusion research. We establish standardized evaluation protocols for unsupervised fault detection with normal-only training and supervised fault classification with balanced dataset splits across different operating conditions and fault types. A unified channel-wise kNN baseline is provided to enable fair comparison of representation quality without task-specific training. The dataset offers a practical and extensible benchmark for robust multimodal industrial fault analysis.

items.title: Improving multichannel speech enhancement through accurate room-acoustic simulations
items.authors: Georg Götz(Treble Technologies); Alessia Milo(Treble Technologies); Steinar Guðjónsson(Treble Technologies); Daniel Gert Nielsen(Treble Technologies); Jesper Pedersen(Treble Technologies); Finnur Pind(Treble Technologies)
items.abstract: Room-acoustic simulations are widely used to augment training data for deep-learning-based speech enhancement. While most pipelines rely on simplified geometrical acoustics, wave-based approaches offer greater physical accuracy. In this work, we examine how simulation fidelity affects multichannel speech enhancement performance. To this end, we train SpatialNet on datasets augmented with different room-acoustic simulation methods and evaluate the resulting models on measured data. We compare lower-fidelity datasets based on geometrical acoustics with a high-fidelity dataset using advanced acoustic modelling and a hybrid combination of wave-based and geometrical acoustics simulations. Training on the high-fidelity dataset results in an up to 38% relative reduction in median word error rate compared to the lower-fidelity alternatives. These results show that augmentation with high-fidelity room-acoustic simulations directly translates into improved multichannel speech enhancement performance.

items.title: Data Filtering Trade-offs in Self-Supervised Speech Representation Learning: A Study on Unconstrained Broadcast Audio
items.authors: Yaroslav Getman(Aalto University); Tamás Grósz(Walton Institute); Tommi Lehtonen(Finnish Arts and Culture Agency); Mikko Kurimo(Aalto University)
items.abstract: When processing raw broadcast audio for self-supervised learning (SSL) pretraining, initial filtering decisions include whether to retain only speech and restrict to the target language. While common in prior work, these choices rely on heuristics without systematic evaluation. We present a controlled comparison of 4 filtering strategies of increasing selectivity on Finnish broadcast data: no filtering, energy-based voice activity detection (VAD), neural VAD, and neural VAD with language identification (LID). Energy-based VAD consistently degrades representation quality compared to no filtering. Neural VAD substantially improves ASR, especially when combined with LID (up to 12.7% absolute WER reduction using 42% of the data), but increasingly selective filtering degrades general audio understanding by up to 9 percentage points. We show that no single strategy is universally optimal and quantify trade-offs between preprocessing cost, downstream accuracy, and generalizability.

items.title: Collecting Prosody in the Wild: A Content-Controlled, Privacy-First Smartphone Protocol and Empirical Evaluation
items.authors: Timo K. Koch(University of St. Gallen; LMU Munich); Florian Bemmann(LMU Munich; University of Mannheim); Ramona Schoedel(LMU Munich; University of Psychology); Markus Buehner(LMU Munich); Clemens Stachl(University of St. Gallen)
items.abstract: Collecting everyday speech data for prosodic analysis is challenging due to the confounding of prosody and semantics, privacy constraints, and participant compliance. We introduce and empirically evaluate a content-controlled, privacy-first smartphone protocol that uses scripted read-aloud sentences to standardize lexical content (including prompt valence) while capturing naturalistic variation in prosodic delivery. The protocol performs on-device prosodic feature extraction, deletes raw audio immediately, and transmits only derived features for analysis. We deployed the protocol in a large study (N = 560; 9,877 recordings), evaluated compliance and data quality, and conducted diagnostic prediction tasks on the extracted features, predicting self-reported speaker sex and momentary affective states (valence, arousal). We discuss implications and directions for advancing and deploying the protocol.

items.title: From Game-Based Annotation to Representation Probing: Cross-Validated Prosodic Speech and Privacy Implications
items.authors: Sia Vosh Sepanta(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Roberto Zamparelli(Cimec University of Trento); Alessio Brutti(Fondazione Bruno Kessler)
items.abstract: Building upon a prosodic speech corpus collected through a web-based interactive game, this paper examines its value for analyzing biometric speaker attributes, such as gender and age, and for LLM-level representation analysis. The corpus was designed so that players serve as both performers and annotators, creating a self-validating mechanism in which each utterance is evaluated through independent human judgments. This design enables systematic assessment of annotation consistency and label robustness. We evaluate the corpus through emotion recognition and probing of LLM-aligned speech representations. Results show that prosodic embeddings encode stable affective patterns while emotional attributes remain identifiable in intermediate representations, raising privacy considerations.

items.title: Automatic Curation of Large-Scale, High-Quality, Multi-Category Music Source Separation Dataset
items.authors: Yu Ji(Xiaomi Inc.); Shuo Yang(Xiaomi Inc.); Yuetonghui Xu(Central Conservatory of Music); Mengmei Liu(Xiaomi Inc.); Qiang Ji(Xiaomi Inc.); zerui Han(Xiaomi Inc.)
items.abstract: The scale, audio quality, and granularity of instrument categories in datasets are critical factors limiting the performance of music source separation. Web crawling provides large-scale data but often introduces label noise and mismatches. We propose an automated method for constructing large-scale, high-quality, multi-category music source separation datasets. The approach comprises 4 steps: (1) designing a fine-grained 7-category musical instrument taxonomy; (2) training instrument-specific single-source detectors to identify segments containing only the target instrument; (3) retrieving plenty of raw audio data from public platforms using multilingual keywords; and (4) automatically cleaning the raw data with the detectors to produce a high-quality dataset. Our detector achieves 97.14% average accuracy across seven categories. Training SOTA models with the cleaned data yields an average SDR improvement of 1.16,dB on standard benchmarks, confirming the dataset's effectiveness.

items.title: Leveraging Discriminative Capabilities of Self-Supervised Neural Audio Fingerprinting for Efficient Speech Data Annotation
items.authors: Kemal Altwlkany(Infobip; University of Sarajevo); Elmedin Selmanovic(University of Sarajevo)
items.abstract: Self-supervised neural audio fingerprinting methods have achieved great results in music retrieval systems. We show how such methods can be applied to efficiently organize speech data annotation tasks. First, they can be used to remove duplicates, which we successfully apply to industry-specific data, resulting in halving the number of data samples that need to be annotated. Second, we show that despite being trained only on music, the embeddings produced by neural fingerprinting methods are better at capturing acoustical properties of speech than speech-specific models, such as WavLM. We leverage this property of the embeddings and show how to subsample large datasets while preserving dataset diversity and avoiding biases towards overrepresented data points, using a technique known as farthest point sampling. This allows annotators to focus their already limited and valuable time on diverse data samples while avoiding duplicate and similar samples.

items.title: Cognitive-Heuristic Guided Multimodal Data Augmentation for Alzheimer’s Disease Detection Using LLM and TTS
items.authors: Yu Jiang(Tianjin University); Cheng Gong(TeleAI); Bin Wen(Tianjin University); Ruihao Jing(TeleAI); Tianrui Wang(Tianjin University); Shansong Liu(TeleAI); Boyu Zhu(TeleAI); Yuheng Lu(Tianjin University); Xuanchen Li(Tianjin University); Xiao Wei(Tianjin University); Chunyu Qiang(Tianjin University); Xiao-Lei Zhang(TeleAI); Longbiao Wang(Tianjin University); Jianwu Dang(Tianjin University)
items.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, and early detection is critical for intervention. Speech offers a non-invasive, accessible biomarker for AD detection, but suffers from severe data scarcity. Existing augmentation methods in text or speech enrich training data but often neglect cognitively relevant patterns. We propose a cognitive-heuristic guided multimodal generative augmentation frame work that explicitly incorporates AD-related cognitive declines. Our method integrates retrieval-augmented generation with large language models for cognitively informed text generation, and an attribute-guided text-to-speech system to reproduce AD-related acoustic features. This design captures both linguistic and acoustic alterations associated with cognitive decline. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that our augmented data consistently enhances performance, highlighting the efficacy of cognition-driven multimodal synthesis for speech-based AD detection.
